Three rules to remember

  1. Order: Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number (number of protons / nuclear charge).
  2. Period: The period number tells you how many electron shells are occupied in a ground-state atom.
  3. Main group (A): The A-group number indicates the number of outer-shell electrons for typical main-group elements (IA–VIIIA; helium is an exception). In modern groups 1–18, groups 1–2 have 1–2 outer electrons and groups 13–18 usually have 3–8.
  4. A vs B groups: A groups occupy the left and right sides of the table (groups 1–2, 13–18); B groups occupy the central transition-metal block (groups 3–12). The lanthanides and actinides are displayed separately below.

Memory tip: Period = electron shells; main group A = outer-shell electrons; elements are ordered by increasing atomic number.

Nonmetallic character

Learn one pattern, then test it yourself.

01 / UNDERSTAND

What does nonmetallic character mean?

Nonmetallic character is the property of an element whose atoms readily gain electrons to form negative ions. The more readily its atoms gain electrons to form negative ions, the stronger the element’s nonmetallic character.

QUICK SUMMARY
Nonmetallic character → readily gains electrons (e⁻).
The more readily an atom gains electrons, the stronger its nonmetallic character.
Across a period→Generally increases
Up a group↑Generally increases
02 / NOTICE THE PATTERN
REMEMBER THIS
→Across a period: increases to the right
↑Up a group: increases upward

These are general trends, especially useful for main-group elements.

04 / WATCH ELECTRONS

Two ways electrons behave in bonds

Switch between ionic electron transfer and unequal electron sharing. These are simplified teaching models, not real-time recordings of reactions.

Scientific note: NaCl is an ionic solid, while HCl has a polar covalent H–Cl bond. These are conceptual models: electrons do not travel along fixed circular paths, and the H–Cl pair is shared rather than transferred.

About & Scientific Accuracy

This periodic table is an educational reference. Its animated atomic model is a simplified illustration of electron-shell distribution, not a depiction of real electron trajectories. Scientific measurements may depend on conditions, and some properties—especially for short-lived synthetic elements—are predicted, uncertain, or not yet measured. Not every element profile has been individually verified; consult the linked scientific references before relying on specific values. Atomic weights use CIAAW 2024 abridged values where available; bracketed whole numbers represent isotope mass numbers, not standard atomic weights. The 34 isotope mass numbers have been aligned with the CIAAW/NUBASE2020 reference table; some isotopes have multiple plausible selections.

Authoritative references: IUPAC · Royal Society of Chemistry · NIST
